form.label: 2. Redundant DB Servers — Failover Visibility
form.description: See why a redundant database pair actually failed over — instead of only knowing that it did.

html.blockquote: "Redundante Datenbankserver, die aktuell viel zu wenig überwacht werden. Es kann momentan nicht nachvollzogen werden, wieso sich das redundante System nun aktiviert hat."
html.p: The standby database took over — which is the system doing its job — but there's no monitoring stitched together to say why: was it the primary's CPU/memory, a lost heartbeat over the network, a disk issue, or a manual failover? Without a timeline that lines up the cluster/replication log with the host metrics of both nodes and the network heartbeat between them, every failover becomes its own investigation.

panel.title: Data sources needed to build this for real

ul.li: Database / cluster logs — PostgreSQL (streaming replication + Patroni), SQL Server Always On availability group events, Oracle Data Guard, or Pacemaker/ Corosync cluster logs — the "who is primary now, and why" record.
Host / OS metrics — CPU, memory, disk I/O and load on both primary and standby (the same *_metrics pattern already used in this lab's Host & Infra Metrics dashboard).
Network heartbeat / VIP logs — the keepalive or virtual-IP mechanism the cluster uses to detect the primary is gone (e.g. keepalived, cluster VIP move events).
Application / connection logs — client-side connection errors and reconnects, to size the actual customer/business impact of the failover.

search.query: | makeresults count=1 | eval RootCause="Primary node CPU pegged at 100% for 90s -> missed 3 consecutive heartbeats -> standby promoted" | eval "Primary node"="db-primary-01", "Standby node (now active)"="db-standby-01", "Failover time"=strftime(relative_time(now(),"-38m"),"%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S"), "Missed heartbeats"=3, "Client reconnects (5 min after)"=214 | table "Failover time" "Primary node" "Standby node (now active)" RootCause "Missed heartbeats" "Client reconnects (5 min after)"

panel.title: CPU on both nodes around the failover

search.query: | makeresults count=40 | streamstats count as i | eval Minute=strftime(relative_time(now(), "-".(40-i)."m"), "%H:%M") | eval "db-primary-01 CPU %"=case(i>=18 AND i<=24, 92+ (i%3*2), 1=1, 22+(i%5)) | eval "db-standby-01 CPU %"=case(i>22, 55+(i%6), 1=1, 18+(i%4)) | table Minute "db-primary-01 CPU %" "db-standby-01 CPU %"

| makeresults count=40 | streamstats count as i | eval Minute=strftime(relative_time(now(), "-".(40-i)."m"), "%H:%M") | eval "db-primary-01"=if(i<22,1,0) | eval "db-standby-01"=if(i<22,0,1) | table Minute "db-primary-01" "db-standby-01"

panel.title: The SPL, once cluster logs + host metrics are onboarded

html.pre: (index=db_cluster_logs OR index=*_metrics host IN (db-primary-01, db-standby-01)) | eval role_event=if(sourcetype="cluster:role_change", role, null()) | streamstats window=1 latest(role_event) as current_role by host | stats values(current_role) as role_changes, max(eval(if(sourcetype="linux:metrics",cpu_pct,null()))) as peak_cpu, count(eval(sourcetype="cluster:heartbeat_missed")) as missed_heartbeats by host, _time | where isnotnull(role_changes) OR missed_heartbeats>0
html.p: The goal isn't to stop failovers — it's to answer "why" in seconds instead of hours, and to catch the CPU/heartbeat pattern before the next one triggers.
